cards.title: Riyadh airport attack kills 12 and wounds more than 300
cards.summary: Saudi authorities said a missile attack on Riyadh airport killed 12 people and injured more than 300, prompting a wider aviation and regional-security response.
detail: Saudi civil-aviation authorities said a missile attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh killed 12 people and injured more than 300. Associated Press reported that Saudi Arabia extended the airport closure after the Saturday strike; Reuters-linked reporting described it as the deadliest attack in the kingdom since the current war began.
The immediate consequence is operational: a major civilian hub is closed while airlines and passengers face rerouting, delays, and a new risk signal across the Red Sea and Gulf air corridors.

The casualty figure is attributed to Saudi authorities, while responsibility and the precise damage assessment remain contested in the conflict’s competing accounts. The attack follows earlier Houthi strikes and a wider Saudi-backed campaign in Yemen.

The next checks are airport reopening, independent damage reporting, and whether the United States or Saudi Arabia expands its response. The edition treats the operational and casualty facts as reported, not as a complete military assessment.

cards.title: Trump announces Russian diesel deal as fuel prices stay high
cards.summary: The White House says Russia will supply diesel to U.S. and global markets, a sharp policy reversal whose price impact and implementation remain uncertain.
detail: President Donald Trump said he reached an agreement with Vladimir Putin for Russia to supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel immediately, followed by larger volumes. The next evidence is the formal legal mechanism, shipment timing, sanctions treatment, and verified price response. Ukraine’s objection and the Kremlin’s implementation details remain part of the unresolved record.

cards.summary: The administration suspended Microsoft, Adobe and major IT outsourcers from a labor-certification route for employment-based green cards, citing alleged fraud and worker-protection concerns.

cards.summary: Brussels and Beijing reported understandings on hybrid-car exports, selected tariffs, and rare-earth licensing after two days of trade talks.

The package matters because it addresses the trade imbalance and industrial supply chains at the same time. European manufacturers want access to Chinese markets and critical inputs, while the bloc is trying to limit pressure from Chinese vehicle exports without immediately escalating a wider tariff conflict.

Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič said the hybrid arrangement could cut projected Chinese exports by more than half over four years compared with no policy change. That is an estimate attached to the understanding, not a verified reduction already delivered.

The next test is implementation: the legal text, customs treatment, export-licence operation, and whether member states accept the balance. The initial understanding is real; its durability and industrial effect remain uncertain.

cards.title: EU–China rare-earth access becomes the region’s policy driver
cards.summary: The first trade-rebalancing package pairs a possible cut in Chinese hybrid exports with easier rare-earth licensing and lower tariffs for selected European goods.
detail: The European Commission and independent reporting described an EU–China understanding covering hybrid and plug-in hybrid exports, selected tariff reductions, and a green channel for rare-earth and permanent-magnet licences. Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič called it an initial step rather than a final settlement.

For European industry, rare-earth access can matter as much as vehicle exports because magnets and other inputs sit inside automotive, energy, and electronics supply chains. The policy is therefore both a trade and industrial-capacity signal.

The possible export reduction is an estimate attached to the understanding, not a delivered volume change. Market cards should distinguish the Commission’s projection from measured shipments and prices.
The next evidence is the final text, customs practice, and licence approvals. The deal’s durability remains uncertain.
